{{Short description|Cognitive bias}}

'''Zero-risk bias''' is a tendency to prefer the complete elimination of [[risk]] in a sub-part over alternatives with greater ''overall'' risk reduction.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JoRQDAAAQBAJ&q=Zero-risk+bias+elimination+of+risk&pg=PT122|title=The Laws of Wealth: Psychology and the secret to investing success|last=Crosby|first=Daniel|date=2016-06-27|publisher=Harriman House Limited|isbn=9780857195258|language=en}}</ref> It often manifests in cases where decision makers address problems concerning health, safety, and the environment.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=ProjectThink: Why Good Managers Make Poor Project Choices|last1=Virine|first1=Lev|last2=Trumper|first2=Michael|publisher=Routledge|year=2016|isbn=9781409454984|location=Oxon|pages=102, 175}}</ref> Its effect on [[decision making]] has been observed in [[Survey sampling|surveys]] presenting hypothetical scenarios.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Monetizing Your Data: A Guide to Turning Data into Profit-Driving Strategies and Solutions|last1=Wells|first1=Andrew Roman|last2=Chiang|first2=Kathy|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|year=2017|isbn=9781119356240|location=Hoboken, NJ|pages=143}}</ref>

== Explanation ==
Zero-risk bias is based on the way people feel better if a risk is eliminated instead of being merely mitigated.<ref name=":1" /> Scientists identified a zero-risk bias in responses to a questionnaire about a hypothetical cleanup scenario involving two hazardous sites X and Y, with X causing 8 cases of cancer annually and Y causing 4 cases annually. The respondents ranked three cleanup approaches: two options each reduced the total number of cancer cases by 6, while the third reduced the number by 5 while eliminating the cases at site Y. While the latter option featured the worst reduction overall, 42% of the respondents ranked it better than at least one of the other options. This conclusion resembled one from an earlier economics study that found people were willing to pay high costs to eliminate a risk.<ref name="BGK 1993">{{cite journal |url=http://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/gowda.html |title=Attitudes toward managing hazardous waste: What should be cleaned up and who should pay for it? |first1=Jonathan |last1=Baron |first2=Rajeev |last2=Gowda |author-link3=Howard Kunreuther|first3=Howard |last3=Kunreuther |year=1993 |journal=Risk Analysis |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=183–192 |doi=10.1111/j.1539-6924.1993.tb01068.x|bibcode=1993RiskA..13..183B |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="VMH 1987">{{cite journal |title=An investigation of the rationality of consumer valuation of multiple health risks |first1=W. K. |last1=Viscusi |first2=W. A. |last2=Magat |first3=J. |last3=Huber |journal=RAND Journal of Economics |year=1987 |volume=18 |issue=4 |pages=465–479 |jstor=2555636 |hdl=1803/6944 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> It has a [[normative]] justification since once risk is eliminated, people would have less to worry about and such removal of worry also has utility.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Thinking and Deciding|last=Baron|first=Jonathan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2003|isbn=978-0521659727|location=Cambridge|pages=506}}</ref> It is also driven by our preference for winning much more than losing as well as the old instead of the new way, all of which cloud the way the world is viewed.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JoRQDAAAQBAJ&q=%22zero-risk+bias%22&pg=PT122|title=The Laws of Wealth: Psychology and the secret to investing success|last=Crosby|first=Daniel|date=2016-06-27|publisher=Harriman House Limited|isbn=9780857195258|location=Hampshire, UK|language=en}}</ref>

Multiple real-world policies have been said to be affected by this bias. In American federal policy, the [[Delaney clause]] outlawing cancer-causing additives from foods (regardless of actual risk) and the desire for perfect cleanup of [[Superfund]] sites have been alleged to be overly focused on complete elimination. Furthermore, the effort needed to implement zero-risk laws grew as technological advances enabled the detection of smaller quantities of hazardous substances. Limited resources were increasingly being devoted to low-risk issues.<ref name="Kunreuther 1991">{{cite journal |url=http://opim.wharton.upenn.edu/risk/downloads/archive/arch156.pdf |title=Managing hazardous waste: past, present and future |first=Howard |last=Kunreuther |year=1991 |journal=Risk Analysis |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=19–26 |doi=10.1111/j.1539-6924.1991.tb00561.x |bibcode=1991RiskA..11...19K |archive-date=2010-06-19 |access-date=2012-10-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100619182913/http://opim.wharton.upenn.edu/risk/downloads/archive/arch156.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Critics of the zero-risk bias model cite that it has the tendency to neglect overall risk reduction. For instance, when eliminating two side effects, it holds that the complete eradication of just one side-effect is preferable to lowering the overall risk.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Perceived Safety: A Multidisciplinary Perspective|last1=Raue|first1=Martina|last2=Streicher|first2=Bernhard|last3=Lermer|first3=Eva|publisher=Springer|year=2019|isbn=9783030114541|location=Cham, Switzerland|pages=65}}</ref>

== Causes ==
Other biases might underlie the zero-risk bias. One is a tendency to think in terms of [[ratio|proportion]]s rather than differences. A greater reduction in proportion of deaths is valued higher than a greater reduction in actual deaths. The zero-risk bias could then be seen as the extreme end of a broad bias about quantities as applied to risk. [[Framing effect]]s can enhance the bias, for example, by emphasizing a large proportion in a small set, or can attempt to [[cognitive bias mitigation|mitigate the bias]] by emphasizing total quantities.<ref name="Baron 2003">{{cite journal |url=http://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/ratsymp.html |title=Value analysis of political behavior - self-interested : moralistic :: altruistic : moral |first1=Jonathan |last1=Baron |year=2003 |journal=University of Pennsylvania Law Review |volume=151 |issue=3 |pages=1135–1167 |doi=10.2307/3312887|jstor=3312887 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
